To accomplish this, we propose a new NLI dataset, referred to as $VERBI$, which is centered around verb meanings and tailored to align with these theoretical specifications. Comprising 198,824 sentence pairs, the dataset examines the NLI categories through the lens of verb meanings. It distinguishes between two key aspects: the semantic meaning of NLI categories and how they are connected, much like the analysis in (Borscheid et al., 2019), which highlights the varying levels of intimacy between the speaker and the event described by a sentence. This distinction enables the development of more precise NLI labels that capture the diverse relationships between PREMISE SPEAKER EVENT speaker, the event described by a sentence, and how the speaker interacts with the event. By doing so, we seek to promote a better comprehension of NLI categories and their connections. Furthermore, we introduce enhancements to current NLI training techniques. By incorporating the semantic relationships between NLI categories and enhancing the contrastive learning approach, we aim to reduce the gap between NLI performance and the improved understanding of verb meanings. This research is based on extensive experiments conducted on seven state-of-the-art NLI models, where we observe a notable 4.1% and 3.3% increase in accuracy within the full and weak settings, respectively. Even with the improved training methodology, a notable disparity between the NLI performance and the accurate interpretation of verb meanings remains, which is attributed to the inherent complexities of natural language and the limitations of current models. Consequently, the $VERBI$ dataset is made publicly available to facilitate future advancements in NLI that align with the improved understanding of verb meanings. This research is open-source and can be accessed at https://github.com/SEAL-UNIL/VERBI. Additionally, the $VERBI$ dataset can be found at https://seal-unil.github.io/VERBI/index.html. one of the most popular AI techniques used to solve various graph-related problems, including anomaly and fault diagnosis. This method has achieved significant success in multiple applications. However, conventional GNN-based methods often rely on neighborhood aggregation to handle node features, which can lead to overemphasized role of neighboring nodes in the feature aggregation process. This may result in difficulties in effectively combining the feature of a given node with its remote neighbors. To address this issue, we propose a novel method called multi-scale graph neural network (mGNN) that incorporates an extended self-attention mechanism to capture the feature interactions across different scales. By utilizing a stack of convolutional layers with varying kernel sizes, we enable the network to extract node features at various scales and then utilize a self-attention mechanism to selectively combine the features of remote nodes. Experimental results on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate the superior performance of mGNN against state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, the case studies on fault diagnosis validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The mGNN code will be available upon request.

A practical implementation of this theory is also demonstrated through the development of an algorithm for detecting limit cycles in a specific class of 2D dynamical systems. Finally, this report showcases the efficacy of this algorithm using a range of nonlinear system examples. Its results indicate that the algorithm effectively detects limit cycles across various relative amplitudes and system scales, even in cases where high-dimensional embeddings are required. All of these detection outcomes are rigorously justified by theoretical proofs. Furthermore, a refinement is proposed to enhance the algorithm's accuracy in cases where precise limit cycle tracking is necessary. Its validation using multiple system examples confirms its reliability and efficient operation. Lastly, a global stability assessment for the first-order Hopf bifurcation is also performed, offering a novel perspective on nonlinear system phase-space dynamics. Ultimately, this study contributes to advancing both numerical and analytical methods for detecting limit cycles in dynamical systems. Its methods are adaptable for detecting other nonlinear system features, such as hidden oscillations in complex dynamics, as well as providing a foundation for extending these detection algorithms to other types of systems. Its global approach also facilitates detecting limit cycles in several important engineering system examples, such as the Van der Pol oscillator and a simplified model of the vertical movement of a pendulum, among others. Its implementation using Python is available at https://github.com/vzeqar/Detect-LC. Its global algorithm is characterized by its reliability (true positives: 100%, false positives: 0%), high accuracy (mean absolute error: 0.71%), and optimal performance (mean relative difference: 0.74%). Its duration is averaged at 0.157 seconds. These results surpass the existing detector performance in many system features. This report demonstrates two principal contributions: Firstly, a revised explanation is offered for the genesis of the Ghoussoub-Preiss condition through an "extremal translation" concept, aiming to clarify the condition's nature. Secondly, an alternative proof is presented for a result by Allen-Bickle, linking the condition to a situation where a convex function's graph encompasses an open set containing an analytic cone. This report further details an analysis of the condition's implications for its application in proving the global smooth embedding of certain compact domains into R^n. No assumptions are made regarding the convex function being lower semi-convex in this context. Finally, an exploration is provided of possible relaxations of the condition, encompassing the treatment of " Dirac issues" that arise when the function's gradient vanishes at isolated points. Such relaxations open up avenues for generalizing the condition and, by extension, the theory of C^1 closure of relatively compact domains in R^n. Several promising avenues for further research are identified. Above all, this report aims to offer a didactic "first encounter" with the Ghoussoub-Preiss condition, aiming to illuminate and demystify this crucial theoretical tool.  This report is based on talks given at the 20th Southeastern Analytical Seminar and the 2022 Southeastern Analytical Seminar, along with an in-depth lecture provided at the University of British Columbia's Spring-Summer 2022 School on Geometric PDEs.  Various key references have been incorporated at the report's conclusion.  It is my hope that this report will serve as a beneficial introduction for those who are encountering the Ghoussoub-Preiss identity for the first time.

Built with a pixel sensor and a thin silicon material, this telescope captures particle trajectories in real-time via a readout chip. Testing confirmed its ability to accurately record particle positions and velocities with transverse resolutions of 50 micrometers and time resolutions of 5 picoseconds, respectively. Due to its compact size and low power consumption, this telescope is well-suited for portable and battery-powered applications, including the DARWIN dark matter detector and the Square Kilometre Array radio telescope. In this research, two modified versions of the Pixel Luminosity Telescope were created using the FE-I4 and FE-I6 readout chips produced by the ATLAS sensor manufacturer. Both prototypes successfully demonstrated their ability to operate within a 50 MHz to 60 MHz readout frequency range, consistent with the expected rates at the LHC. Experimental results indicate that the Pixel Luminosity Telescope can be reliably fabricated using the components of a particle detector, thereby validating the manufacturer's specifications in the context of the ATLAS detector. Furthermore, this research presented novel operational techniques for the Pixel Luminosity Telescope, including an improved clock design and a linear feedback approach to maintain consistent pixel readout. Finally, two design refinements were proposed to further optimize the Pixel Luminosity Telescope's performance: first, a partitioned logical ring counter for the FE-I4 chip; second, an optimized 30 R-2D match filter for the FE-I6 chip. Lastly, the research concluded by outlining potential use cases for the Pixel Luminosity Telescope. Typically, LMs are optimized for a single objective function that might not adequately represent the diverse range of linguistic inputs it will encounter. In this study, we propose a multi-objective optimization framework that simultaneously trains multiple language models, each specialized in processing a particular type of linguistic input, with the goal of jointly maximizing their performance in predicting the correct output. Our framework is based on the Multi-Fidelity Performance Estimation technique that helps in achieving a precise balance between the performance and the cost of the trained models. In this research, we experiment with training multiple LMs using a dataset of English sentences, categorizing them into five distinct groups based on the length of the context and the presence of special tokens. We evaluate our proposed approach, comparing it to the standard baseline technique that trains a single, comprehensive LM, in terms of its ability to predict the correct output when the input text is an image caption. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed multi-objective optimization framework can significantly improve the SOTA performance, delivering an overall improvement of 2.9 F1 score or 0.9 ROGUE score. A key challenge in this field is the scarcity of labeled data, which complicates the process of image manipulation through direct prediction of target pixels.  A promising approach to image manipulation is single-image conditional adversarial network (SICAN), which sequentially applies a series of conditional adversarial networks to achieve the desired results. This paper introduces the concept of self-expressiveness into the optimization process of SICAN to facilitate efficient image transformation. This paper examines the performance of machine learning algorithms using photoplethysmographic signal data obtained from wearable devices. Our investigation centers around oxygen saturation's fluctuating component, which we treat as a time series problem. We evaluate the capabilities of three machine learning models – Random Forest, XGBoost, and a neural network – to extract relevant features from the PPG signal. A subsequent study using a Pearson correlation analysis and statistical testing with a t-test and ANOVA compares the accuracy of these models in predicting oxygen saturation levels. Our findings reveal that a neural network predicts the saturation levels of a test patient with an average MSE of 0.031, comparing favorably to the other methods. Additionally, the study discusses the efficacy of feature extraction using machine learning algorithms in predicting spO2 from the PPG signal. Our analysis ultimately led to the selection of a neural network optimized with the GridSearch parameter tuning technique from the scikit-learn library in Python. This paper presents an enhanced version of the open-source ESPFF project, which features an open-source Python code for processing spO2 from the PPG signal using machine learning algorithms.   setting. Domain adaptation focuses on learning a model from data of one 
  domain with the expectation that it will perform well on another domain. 
  Given the scarcity of data in domain adaptation, using deep neural networks for 
  generative modeling becomes even more complicated. This study therefore examines
  the effectiveness of deep neural networks for generative modeling in the 
  domain adaptation setting using limited data. We evaluate four different 
  approaches: one-class classification, adversarial networks, representation 
  learning, and autoencoders. Our analysis reveals that adversarial networks 
  perform better than the other methods when it comes to adapting models from 
  source domains to target domains. Additionally, we find that increasing the 
  availability of labeled target data improves the performance of adversarial 
  networks. Furthermore, by comparing different network architectures for 
  image domain adaptation, we discover that reverse gradient adversarial networks 
  achieve better results than Gan-based domain adaptation and cycle-gan. Our 
  analysis also highlights how the performance of deep neural networks varies 
  depending on the data availability in target domain, with domain adaptation 
  networks performing better than independent models when there is limited 
  target data. Moreover, in functional domain adaptation with limited target data, 
  deep neural networks achieve better results than independent models when there 
  is no target data. Ultimately, domain adaptation networks perform better than 
  one-class classification when there is no target data. Last but not least, by

These studies have concentrated on the structural properties of vortices as a function of latitude. In our research, we expand upon this analysis by exploring the temporal dynamics of these vortices in daily time-series data from three different sources: visual and automated methods from raw satellite images, and a complex geophysical reanalysis model. We compare the temporal coherence of these vortices in both quasi-equilibrium and dynamic contexts, leveraging the network structure of these systems to distinguish vortex lifetimes and spatial interconnections. Our results indicate that ensemble statistics in time-series data are insufficient for accurately modeling vortex behavior over long periods. Instead, understanding the discrete nature of these complex systems in both space and time requires investigating the dynamic coupling between vortices and surrounding networks. By topologically examining pair-wise vortex connections, we have developed a new metric for quantifying and interpreting vortex identification method biases. Our research provides a framework for validating vortex identification algorithms through discrete space and time analysis, ultimately enhancing our comprehension of vortex-induced rainfall localization and discrete atmospheric pattern occurrence. in data-driven information systems is nearly universal, with ML models serving most online platforms with tasks such as content curation, advertising, e-commerce product recommendations, and social media post dissemination. Among these systems, ML algorithms govern the decision-making processes that shape our daily interactions with technology. Despite the significant impact of these systems on society, their decision-making processes lack transparency. This gap in understanding is attributed to the use of complex ML algorithms and data that are considered proprietary by the companies operating these systems. Furthermore, the lack of clear guidelines on how to develop and evaluate ML-enabled decision support systems (DSS) contributes to the persistence of this knowledge gap. This research aims to develop a foundation for an open and transparent DSS by leveraging human-centered AI development methods. The proposed methodology comprises three core components: (1) monitoring ML system outputs to extract knowledge, (2) crowd-sensing to gather users' perspectives on ML-based DSS, and (3) applying transparency-enhancing algorithms to the underlying ML algorithms. The methodology enables the empirical evaluation of a data-driven DSS by measuring user acceptance of the system and its decision outputs. The research presents results from experiments conducted on a DSS used for content curation within social media platforms. The findings show that users trust ML-powered DSS more when their decision outputs are explained or when their input data is returned with explanations. Additionally, the results indicate that users' views on the DSS can shift from negative to positive when the ML algorithm used is replaced with a transparent alternative. This research sheds light on users' roles in developing and evaluating ML-enabled DSS, and it proposes an open ML approach that combines crowd-sensed knowledge with algorithmic transparency. The findings demonstrate that users can participate effectively in governing the DSS by deciding between algorithms that are either data-driven or user-centered in their decision outputs. The empirical evaluation of the DSS also demonstrates that a data-driven DSS can remain user-centered when its decision outputs are explained or when its input data is returned with explanations. The research contributes theoretical, methodological, and applied values. At a theoretical level, the research provides insights into human-centered AI development, the concept of algorithmic transparency, and users' roles in governing ML-enabled DSS. The methodology proposed can be replicated across various DSS and the findings can be extended to other contexts. Moreover, the research initiates a new line of research focused on evaluating the transparency of ML algorithms and their decision outputs. At a practical level, the research enables users to decide which ML algorithms to employ in

The measured response of Si within its 263-373 K temperature range did not exhibit any features that correlate with the 183 K lattice collapse seen in $^{10}$B-doped silicon. Instead, a broad inelastic peak that resembles a power-law was observed, where it follows that $S(\bfQ,\omega)\propto \omega^{-\gamma}$ with $\gamma$ equal to 1.18, and the form of this power-law remains consistent across the studied Q-range. These findings indicate that Si exhibits amorphous-like behavior, where the obtained power-law is significantly different from the expected $q$-dependent behavior predicted by a theory based on a $J_1-J_2$ antiferromagnetic model. A comparison with existing data for Si, as well as other materials, including $^{10}$B-doped silicon compounds, shows that the obtained results are self-consistent and compatible with a temperature-dependent quantum percolation threshold at 11.5 K, and the presence of a static spin disorder above this threshold. A theoretical model that explains the amorphous-like Si behavior is also proposed, where it is based on a collection of $t$ and $t'$-ordered Si spins that are arranged in a labile ordered framework that is stable at high temperatures due to quantum mechanical effects. Moreover, based on the obtained $\omega/Q$ ratios and the form of the power-law, a detailed analysis of the wavevector-dependent behavior of Si is performed, and the findings indicate a near-neighboring $t'$-correlation that is similar to that observed in a $^{10}$B-doped silicon single-crystal silicon in its 280 K cubic structure, which possesses a significantly larger correlation length than that predicted by a theory based on a $t$-dominated $J_1-J_2$ antiferromagnetic model. A comprehensive overview of the obtained results, combined with existing Si data, is given, and the theoretical implications of these findings are discussed, where the observations support a point-contact quantum percolation model that applies across the studied Q-range, along with a proposal for the Si spin behavior based on a $t'$-dominated $t$-ordered Si framework that is stable at high temperatures due to quantum mechanical effects, where the near-neighboring $t'$-correlation is responsible for the power-law response observed in the Si Si spectrum.

To prevent these breaches, developers continually audit the growing number of smart contracts, with the help of automated tools.  Although these tools reduce human auditing workload, they still yield false positive results that necessitate further review by developers.  To further optimize auditing, we introduce a novel approach utilizing natural language processing and machine learning on smart contract comments extracted from Ethereum's blockchain records.  Our model, which classifies smart contracts as secure or security-breaching based on their comments, outperforms existing benchmarks in prediction efficiency, with an accuracy of 75.7% compared to a random guess.  Our study is the first to explore the application of natural language processing in smart contract auditing, with a second contribution being an open-source dataset containing smart contract comments, which facilitates future research in the field.  Furthermore, we establish a new benchmark for natural language processing models called SPC, with a third contribution being a set of 1,500 translated smart contract comments into English from various languages to ensure the practical usability of the field.  Finally, we conduct a thorough analysis on the linguistic characteristics of smart contract comments in the SPC dataset, with our findings showing that smart contract comments significantly deviate from general text conversations in key aspects, including grammar, punctuation, and sentence length.  This unique trait could entice the development of specialized models tailored to smart contract comments, with our analysis and the SPC dataset encouraging future research in the field.  The study's results are discussed, with our code and the SPC dataset made available for further research.  The models for HST are also made available. Current research focuses on stable and non-stable states of walking and climbing, categorizing them into steady state gaits and transient phases such as walking, climbing, and falling. Absorption Near Edge Spectroscopy (XANES) provide researchers with precise insight into the atomic environment of specified elements within materials. XANES spectra typically exhibit significant sensitivity to particles with diameters of 5-10 nm, making even low concentrations of trace particles in solutions potentially detectable. To verify the existence of such trace particles in solutions, we conducted a series of experiments using a nanocrystalline standard sample to measure the background noise of XANES spectra. Our research involved measuring the spectra of solutions containing known concentrations of tracer particles at varying dilution levels, then applying the fundamentals of signal processing to evaluate the detection threshold for the particles. Our study concluded that particles with diameters of 5-10 nm can be reliably detected in solutions when the concentration of the tracer reaches a level of 10^-4 M or lower. However, it's also found that solutions can introduce significant background noise that may obstruct the detection of trace particles, and that the effectiveness of particle detection heavily depends on the specific shape of the XANES spectra. Furthermore, the data also indicates a potential need to revisit the current theoretical models used to analyze XANES spectra. The research also discussed several practical applications that may utilize the capabilities of XANES to detect extremely dilute solutions, including biochemical and physical studies. Additionally, the paper also mentioned the potential capabilities of combining XANES with other spectroscopic techniques such as Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) to gain a more comprehensive understanding of the atomic environment of specified elements. Finally, the paper also discussed the research limitations and identified several areas where further investigations are required. The analysis also highlights the potential research abilities that may enable the detection of solid state dilute solutions. The analysis also based on experimental data collected from S. Stotz's data published in 2004 in J. Phys. Chem. B, volume 108, issue 26, pp. 11561-11571. A discussion on detecting free metal atoms is also presented. Conversely, the dynamo theory's opposing effect, i.e., the fragmentation of magnetic activity due to excessive velocity is known as the quenching phenomenon. This theory is widely applied to both solar and stellar activity. Nevertheless, researchers have long used global simplifications to model stellar magnetic activity, despite these models being incompatible with the principle of non-linear fragmentation. In order to accurately model stellar magnetic activity, it is essential to use a three-dimensional, non-linear dynamo theory that is consistent with the principle of non-linear fragmentation. This study utilizes three-dimensional numerical simulations of a stellar external convective flow to model stellar magnetic activity, thereby confirming the prediction that as the magnetic activity increases with convective energy input, it will eventually reach a ceiling due to excessive velocity, thereby confirming the principle of non-linear fragmentation. This study also makes available a comprehensive database of stellar magnetic activity in three-dimensional states, which is accessible through the ICRAR's Hi-GAL database website. Furthermore, these results have a range of implications that extend beyond the model itself, including the fact that as a star's mass increases, its magnetic activity should exhibit a particular pattern of growth, as well as indicating the possibility that some stellar magnetic activity could be a result of remnants from stellar formation processes. Finally, these results have implications for the task of inversion that is involved in reconstructing external convective flow and magnetic activity from observational data, including observations of stellar activity cycles and the mass of the stellar companion to the solar system, Proxima Centauri. This study is significant because it is the first to use a three-dimensional, non-linear dynamo theory that is consistent with the principle of non-linear fragmentation to model stellar magnetic activity, thereby making it a major breakthrough in the field of stellar research. Additionally, these results are valuable due to their applicability to stellar models of all masses, from those that are similar to the Sun to supermassive stars that are thought to exist in certain star clusters. Lastly, these results are important because they will be utilized in the analysis of observational data of stellar activity, including data that will be collected with the future generation of telescopes, namely the Extremely Large Telescope (Elt). This study is significant because it is a crucial step towards a more in-depth and complex model of stellar magnetic activity that uses the non-linear dynamo theory, which will help researchers understand stellar activity better and inform the analysis of observational data of stellar activity, including data

Although they are highly effective, RNNs suffer from a limitation known as memory leakage, where the model retains information from previous sequences, which is undesirable in scenarios such as language modeling or speech recognition.  This issue is significant, as consecutive inputs often have distinct characteristics, necessitating a reset of the hidden state.  This problem can be addressed by utilizing an attention module in conjunction with an error-correcting code.  By integrating an attention module, the model's dependence on the entire input sequence is eliminated, and when coupled with an error-correcting code, the model's memory leakage is eliminated, allowing it to reset the hidden state for each new sequence.  This combination is drawn from the applications of both technologies, where the attention module is utilized to extract relevant information from the input sequence, and the error-correcting code is employed to rectify errors in the hidden state.  This combination is theoretically capable of resolving memory leakage in RNNs, and is applicable to a broad range of sequential models, including Correlated RNNs, Higher Order RNNs, and Neural Networks with local feedback connections.  By utilizing this combination, the model's performance is significantly enhanced, and it achieves a level of processing parallelism similar to that of Transformer networks.  This is particularly beneficial in scenarios where the model is unable to access the entire input sequence, which is often the case in applications such as automatic speech recognition or natural language modeling. This test has proven to be robust across diverse datasets, but issues arise when dealing with dataset size, specifically when n is larger than 1250. This larger dataset size causes a significant increase in computational requirements. Consequently, this presents a challenge in statistics for several reasons. Firstly, the increased computational demands make the process slow. Secondly, running this test on large datasets is often impractical due to memory constraints, as it necessitates substantial memory to process the results. Lastly, any errors made in the program due to incorrect rank calculations can significantly skew the outcomes, but it's difficult to identify these mistakes with large datasets as the errors are hard to spot. This thesis proposes an innovative algorithm founded on the principles of C++ efficiency, which successfully overcomes these challenges by efficiently calculating the ranks, splitting the test into smaller components, and optimizing memory usage. As a result, this algorithm significantly boosts performance - achieving a speedup of approximately 7 times when compared to the standard method. An accurate accuracy analysis of the new algorithm was conducted by comparing its results with the results from the statistical package R, utilizing 30 diverse datasets, 10 of which were derived from real-world data, while the remaining 20 were artificially generated with varying program sizes (n). Interestingly, the experiments revealed that the new algorithm produced more accurate outcomes when dealing with program sizes (n) not exceeding 1250. Conversely, the statistical package R showed better results for program sizes (n) greater than 1250. Ultimately, the proposed algorithm has been successfully implemented and is now available as an open-source addition to the Cantor-Dixon rank correlation test. This test is useful in statistics and data analysis and is often utilized in the analysis of real-world datasets. As such, the program is part of the Sigma package version 4.1.2 and can be accessed from the official distribution website. Furthermore, the source code of the algorithm is available at the link provided. Lastly, the artificially generated datasets utilized in the accuracy analysis are available for public use at the specified link. These datasets are comprised of a combination of real-world and artificially generated program sizes (n) to ensure the development of effective rank calculation algorithms. Ultimately, the primary goal of this research was to overcome the challenges of efficient rank correlation test calculation for large dataset sizes, but it has also contributed to the statistical field by providing 20 diverse datasets for future study.

As the temperature difference increases with altitude in the direction perpendicular to the rotation axis, it induces an increase in the shear of the background strain rate. This leads to the spontaneous generation of zonal jets through the baroclinic instability even in the absence of initial disturbances. Our analytical solutions reveal that the growth rate of the instability is directly proportional to the square of the temperature difference. Furthermore, the resulting jet structures exhibit an equilibrium that is self-similar and asymmetric, with variations in the poloidal direction that are out of phase with each other in the zonal direction. Conversely, when the rotation rate surpasses a certain threshold, which varies depending on the temperature difference, the instability becomes suppressed. Our research provides insight into the dynamics of the interaction between the balance of rotation and baroclinic processes in the atmosphere. Our findings have implications for the ability of baroclinic instability to contribute to the formation of persistent and strong zonal jets, which are prevalent in various atmospheric and oceanic flows. an equilibrated quark-gluon plasma in high-energy heavy-ion collisions is modeled using a relativistic quantum field theory, equilibration coefficient theory, which incorporates a theoretical framework for describing the plasma's physical properties. This theoretical model relies on the assumption that the plasma is in a state of equilibrium. A specific theoretical coefficient, the transport scattering coefficient, determines the rate at which particles interact and reach equilibrium. Calculations of the dilepton production rate and comparisons with experimental data reveal that the equilibrium model provides a reasonable estimate of the observed results at intermediate energies. Furthermore, the applicability of the equilibrium model to describe particle production in collisions has a well-established foundation in quantum field theory. Nonetheless, an underlying physical process that is inherent to any equilibrium state contributes substantially to the predicted particle production rates, particularly at low energies. Consequently, these rates are significantly overestimated. Consequently, this may lead to an incorrect understanding of the system's properties if an incorrect theoretical model is used to describe the data. A novel approach to troubleshooting this issue is outlined, which may also contribute to a better understanding of the system's behavior at low energies. A methodology for identifying and removing process contributions from the coefficients is presented, along with an analysis of coefficients for various particles produced in high-energy collisions. Interestingly, the study finds that while some coefficients are significantly affected by the process, others are relatively insulated from its influence. Ultimately, the study demonstrates that the equilibrium model remains a viable theoretical framework for describing particle production in high-energy collisions, particularly at high energies where the influential process is minimal, but it must be further refined to accurately account for the system's behavior at low energies. Additionally, the study highlights the potential for equilibration coefficient theory to provide insight into the phase transition between the quark-gluon plasma and hadronic matter. Further research is required to fully realize this potential. Through a series of simulations, the study explores the behavior of equilibration coefficients for various plasma components, including baryons, leptons, and photons, across a range of temperatures from approximately 150 MeV to 600 MeV. A distinct, non-monotonic trend is observed for baryon transport coefficients, which is primarily driven by the behavior of nucleons and antinucleons. In contrast, the behavior of electron, muon, and photon transport coefficients is more straightforward, exhibiting a generally increasing or decreasing trend in line with temperature expectations, although some discrepancies with theoretical models are found at intermediate temperatures. Initially, we consider the case where the particle has a constant velocity and an initial perpendicular displacement from its parent beam, leading to the formation of a "photonic halo" around the beam's central axis. Within the context of possible quantum interpretations of gravity, we suggest that this photonic halo could play a significant role, and also explore its general properties when the parent beam is focused or within a plasma environment. Furthermore, under specific conditions, when the particle's perpendicular displacement is constant, its radiation forms a circular polarization pattern, leading to the formation of a "polarized ring" around the beam's central axis. We have experimentally verified the concept of the photonic halo through the observation of a "edge darkening" effect in a free-electron laser's output spectrum, and discuss its implications for further research studies. This novel radiation phenomenon, comprising both the photonic halo and polarized ring, opens up wide avenues for the development of innovative charge-modulated free-electron laser devices and related scientific applications. 
  The concept of the photonic halo as a tool for testing quantum gravity could be compromised by its inability to form when the particle is part of the parent beam or travels along a parallel path. However, this issue can be overcome by employing a helical beam or introducing a slight longitudinal displacement for one of the particles. This modified approach allows the photonic halo to facilitate a direct observation of the gravitational force acting between charged particles, a capability that could be leveraged to create a quantum-gravity-based radiation source. 
  We have also successfully tested the feasibility of using the photonic halo for enhancing the efficiency of free-electron lasers by modulating their charge levels. This innovative strategy, involving the exploitation of a "dark-state enhancement," allows for a noticeable improvement in the lasers' output in the undulator region and significant increases in their overall radiation levels. 
  Lastly, within the context of a theoretical quantum gravity model, we have calculated the properties of the photonic halo when particles exhibit a near-zero rest mass, accompanied by the derivation of a crucial inequality that could lead to a quantum-gravity discovery through observations of the photonic halo's characteristics. 
  Finally, we have determined the parameters required for a realistic photonic-halo-based radiation source to be generated, along with a discussion of the inherent limitations to its production. 
  This study has also validated the reliability of our in-house code "Patches"

not 100% compliant. In this paper, we develop a theoretical framework for
analyzing the impact of non-uniform social distancing measures on containment
of an infectious epidemic. Our framework reveals that the ultimate size of the
outbreak is directly proportional to the average of the social distancing
efficacy values in the population. Building on this insight, we adapt the
Kermack-McKendrick-von Bertalanffy model to predict the epidemic's progression
and estimate the ultimate number of infected individuals. Our model also
allows us to determine the time at which the epidemic peaks and to identify
critical population subsets that drive the secondary spread of the epidemic.
  Using this framework, we demonstrate the effectiveness of non-uniform
social distancing interventions in containing the epidemic, even when a large
portion of the population does not comply with the measures. Specifically, we
find that the cumulative incidence of the epidemic can be reduced by up to
80%
even if only 20% of the population follows the instructions for social
distancing. Our work also emphasizes the significance of timely and early
implementation of social distancing measures in the initial stages of the
epidemic. It is essential to act within the first two to three doubling periods
-- a time frame that is directly correlated with the epidemic's latent period.
  In the context of the COVID-19 pandemic in India, which was caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus with a latent period of around 3-4 days, our model suggests that the
critical period for the effective intervention by social distancing began on
March 13, 2020, and ended on March 27, 2020. If social distancing had been
implemented sooner, it is likely that the pandemic's severity in India could
have been reduced. These findings are further validated by the actual
government responses to the pandemic in India, which showed an improvement in
cumulative incidence after the implementation of social distancing measures.

interventions in containing the severity of the epidemic, especially when the
population is non-uniform in its susceptibility to the infection. It is a
revealing example of how such measures can be effective, even when they are
not 100% compliant. Additionally, our work may contribute to a more

Different types of anisotropic cosmological models are represented using tailored basis functions that facilitate analysis with the cosmological parameters. These models include those with non-flat initial conditions, featuring features of the potential that affect both the scalar and tensor properties. Our analysis employs a combination of observational data, including the latest from the Planck experiment, with considerations for the large-scale structure from the Boomerang dataset and the Lyman-alpha forest. Our findings reveal constraints on the parameters of anisotropic cosmological models, including those with non-flat initial conditions, where the ratio of isothermal coordinates lambda. varies between -1 and 0.2, given the boundary data, assuming a power-law spectrum with n_s = 1. Results show that the anisotropic initial conditions may affect the CMB polarization estimates, with a degree of up to 5% error. Furthermore, the analysis places constraints on the values of lambda. and the amplitude of perturbations A in the case of flat initial conditions, with estimates of lambda. ranging from -0.067 to 0.067 and A from 1.5 x 10^-2 to 1.5 x 10^-2. Additionally, the study includes a detailed examination of how the spherical symmetry of the inflationary potential affects the structure of the universe and the resulting CMB patterns at high and low multipoles. Finally, the analysis concludes with implications of anisotropic initial conditions on the inflationary model, with suggestions of an extended period of single-field inflation following the initial conditions, likely lasting more than 4 e-folds, with an inflationary potential characterized by a linear or quadratic relationship between the field value and the tensor ratio t. in the case of flat initial conditions, or a linear relationship in the case of non-flat initial conditions.   Literature has primarily focused on forecasting future prices, neglecting the underlying price processes and relying on established time series models.
  This study endeavors to comprehend the CC market's dynamics by analyzing its past prices and discovering patterns in price histories.
  We examine the distributions of CC prices, their time series components, and how they relate to the 14 largest CCs by market value.
  Findings reveal that CC prices exhibit leptokurtic behavior, with the majority of variations unexplained by past prices.
  This suggests that other factors, such as new CC creations or existing CC liquidations, substantially influence prices.
  Consequently, stationary sub-series are identified in CC prices, including seasonal and non-seasonal components, providing insight into persistent trends and lasting suppositions in CC markets.
  Our analysis shows that CC prices exhibit a mix of local mean-reverting and local mean-persistent tendencies.
  This study presents a new model capturing the core characteristics of CC prices: a fourth-generation distribution-based time series model incorporating non-Gaussian errors, seasonal effects, and localized self-referential dynamics.
  This model demonstrates superior performance in the Bayesian Akaike information ratio context when compared to traditional AR-type models.
  Our analysis offers fresh insights into CC price formation, shedding light on the inherent complexities of CC prices and their potential uses in machine learning and economics fields.

This review focuses on the relationship between the physical and gauge sectors of the theory, investing the matrix elements of operators between these sectors. In general, these anomalies are naturally suppressed, but in the presence of ALPs, they can be potentially observable.  To induce detection, deconfinement is required to interact with the external magnetic field through a dipole moment, or to generate global magnetic fields via a Josephson effect at the boundary between two adjacent regions of different phases.  The former detection method relies on existing experiments, whereas the latter requires future studies.  In particular, axion-like particle physics offers unique opportunities for the study of global anomalies and their effects on the electroweak sector. machine learning models tend to enjoy certain benefits, including enhanced performance and resistance to overfitting. In this context, we present a novel phenomenon known as "intrinsic overfitting," which refers to a situation where a learning algorithm naturally achieves low generalization error even when using significantly more parameters than training examples. We illustrate this concept through a simple mathematical example and investigate its occurrence across a range of typical models, revealing that intrinsic overfitting is a common phenomenon. In order to understand and exploit intrinsic overfitting, we develop a necessary and sufficient condition for a specific class of models, and then extend it to a broader category of models, establishing a robust generalization error bound in the latter case. Our research reveals that intrinsic overfitting is an intrinsic property of some learning algorithms, and highlights the crucial role of regularization by intrinsic overfitting in promoting robust generalization. Our findings are substantiated through numerous experiments conducted using artificial neural networks, causing many experts to wonder whether their favorite learning algorithms are affected by intrinsic overfitting. Interestingly, our empirical analysis suggests that intrinsic overfitting might be an intrinsic property of gradient descent, which has been a widely employed optimization technique. Our study provides novel insights into the behavior of overparameterized learning algorithms and contributes to our fundamental understanding of robust generalization. In addition, our work opens up significant research opportunities, inviting the exploration of intrinsic overfitting in more complex settings, such as learning with nonconvex functions, using techniques other than gradient descent for optimization, and incorporating noisy and deformable data. Furthermore, our empirical methodology could be further developed to facilitate the cross-validation of intrinsic overfitting across a broader range of learning algorithms. Ultimately, our ultimate aim is to devise more efficient, overparameterized models that excel at generalization by leveraging intrinsic overfitting, potentially reshaping the field of machine learning. Initial evidence suggests that this goal might not be an unachievable dream. Lastly, our appendix compiles our study's primary results and accompanies an additional supplement containing extra details. In the presence of a relatively strong electromagnetic field interacting with the atoms, the structure comprises a sequence of layers, where each contains a specified number of atoms that occupy the same lowest energy state. The space between these layers increases exponentially with the number of layers. The system exhibits a unique characteristic where an added electron instantly occupies the available space within the existing layers, forming a plasma that coalesces into a large, moving droplet at low densities. Given the rapid dissemination of news, the spread of disease, and the spread of viral videos, it is clear that model precision is greatly enhanced by considering the network's underlying structure. Traditionally, researchers distinguished between Markov chain models that incorporate the network and those that do not, reserving the term 'random walk' for the latter. In this paper, we seek to bridge this divide by examining random walks on networks and referring to all models as 'random walks', including those that account for the network's structure. Our aim is to provide a comprehensive overview of random walk-based prediction methods that incorporate the network, drawing from both established and more recent studies. Furthermore, we hope this survey will serve as a foundational guide for researchers and practitioners looking to the network's structure in their modeling. Our discussion is accompanied by a range of empirical evaluations that highlight the benefits of considering the network's structure in random walk-based modeling. By exploring both theoretical and practical applications, we aim to unite the disparate communities of researchers working in this domain. Our view is that random walks on networks, forward chains, and stationary distributions are fundamental concepts that are inherently interconnected. In contrast, traditional Markov chains are viewed as a special case of random walks on empty networks. Our approach to analyzing network models is grounded in a simple theorem that illustrates the relationship between these concepts. In the absence of additional information, we recommend utilizing forward chains for both sampling and prediction tasks. In this survey, we also explore the challenges posed by noisy network data and the empty network paradigm, presenting two sets of experimental results along with novel techniques for addressing these issues. the fundamental theorem of finite representation of groups is presented, utilizing the properties of free profinite groups. The argument draws upon key properties of free profinite groups and their faithful profinite actions, which are explored in the initial sections. By establishing a relationship between subgroups of free profinite groups and their invariants under symmetry, it becomes clear that any subgroup of a free profinite group on a set of n generators must also be determined by an index 2 subgroup of its profinite completion. When coupled with the result that a subgroup of index 2 in the profinite completion does not necessarily maintain the same properties when lifted to the group itself, this indicates that any subgroup of a free profinite group that is normal up to profinite equivalence cannot be maximal. By combining this insight with the process of repeatedly removing normal subgroups until they no longer appear in the profinite closure of the group, it becomes possible to demonstrate the finite representation theorem. Our analysis focuses on the gravitational wave strain spectra, and we investigate the effects of the orbiting object's spin. Our findings indicate that when the spin is significant, the gravitational wave frequency is split into two components, resulting in a characteristic "chirp" pattern lasting around an hour, observable from Earth if the orbiting object has a mass comparable to that of Uranus.
